papers.title: MLL4 regulates palatal salivary gland development
papers.abstract: Palatal glands are minor mucous salivary glands that contribute to oral lubrication and mucosal defense through the secretion of mucus and protective factors such as secretory immunoglobulin A. They are also the most common site of benign and malignant minor salivary gland tumors. Despite their physiological and clinical importance, the molecular mechanisms underlying palatal gland development remain poorly understood. Given the essential role of the epigenetic regulator MLL4 (KMT2D) in craniofacial development, we investigated its role in palatal gland development using a conditional knockout (cKO) mouse model with tissue-specific deletion of Mll4 in the palatal mesenchyme (Mll4fl/fl;Osr2-Cre). Mll4-cKO mice exhibited palatal gland hypoplasia from birth through adulthood, accompanied by ectopic cartilage formation in the soft palate. RNA-seq analysis revealed downregulation of genes and biological processes associated with salivary gland development, branching morphogenesis, and FGF and WNT signaling, together with upregulation of biological processes related to chondrocyte proliferation, consistent with the glandular hypoplasia and ectopic cartilage phenotypes. In situ hybridization and immunofluorescence analyses confirmed reduced mesenchymal Fgf10 expression, decreased epithelial SOX9 and Edar expression, and localized accumulation of SOX9-positive cells within the ectopic cartilage. Ki67 immunostaining demonstrated reduced epithelial cell proliferation without altered apoptosis in Mll4-cKO palatal glands. Collectively, these findings identify MLL4 as an essential epigenetic regulator of palatal gland morphogenesis that coordinates mesenchymal-epithelial signaling while maintaining normal developmental programs within the soft palate.

papers.title: Ribosome remodeling under glucotoxic conditions impairs beta-cell function
papers.abstract: Diabetes develops when pancreatic beta-cells fail to secrete sufficient insulin to meet metabolic demand. Chronic hyperglycemia accelerates beta-cell failure and dysregulates mRNA translation before the onset of endoplasmic reticulum stress, but the underlying mechanisms remain unknown. Here, quantitative mass spectrometry of translating ribosomes isolated from MIN6 cells under control and glucotoxic conditions revealed that sustained high glucose remodels ribosome composition by selectively decreasing Ribosomal Protein Lateral Stalk Subunit P1 (RPLP1) on actively translating ribosomes. Knockdown of RPLP1 in MIN6 cells and in primary islets reduced translation of insulin and impaired glucose-stimulated insulin secretion. Depletion of RPLP1 in vivo led to glucose intolerance. Together, our findings indicate that glucotoxicity remodels beta-cell ribosomes, leading to selective mRNA translation impairment and decreased insulin secretion. This previously unrecognized mechanism linking metabolic overload to beta-cell dysfunction suggests that preserving RPLP1 association with ribosomes could represent a therapeutic strategy for maintaining beta-cell function in diabetes.

papers.title: Candidatus Pannonibacter alzirae sp. nov. isolated from a septic immunocompromised patient in Brazil
papers.abstract: Pannonibacter species. are non-fermentative Gram-stain-negative bacteria, with rare reports of human infections primarily affecting immunocompromised patients. Here, we report the genomic and phenotypic characterization of a novel Pannonibacter species, isolated from a bacteremia episode in a pediatric patient with acute lymphoblastic leukemia in Brazil. Initial characterization of the isolate (here named CBAS 1226) by MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry and 16S ribosomal RNA gene sequencing identified it as Pannonibacter sp., most closely related to P. phragmitetus. However, comparison of its MALDI-TOF spectrum with a commercial reference library revealed compatibility with only two of the five main spectra profiles for P. phragmitetus. This discrepancy motivated comprehensive genomic, biochemical, morphological, and antimicrobial resistance profiling of CBAS 1226. Genomic analysis revealed that Pannonibacter sp. CBAS 1226 is phylogenetically distinct from P. phragmitetus and other known species, with ANI and dDDH values below species delineation thresholds, supporting its proposal as Candidatus Pannonibacter alzirae. It forms small, non-hemolytic, grayish-white colonies on blood agar, similar to its closest relatives P. phragmitetus and P. indicus. Phenotypically, it is distinguished by positive - and {beta}-glucosidase activity, along with the utilization of citrate, L-proline, and 2-ketoglutarate. It is negative for alkaline phosphatase and unable to utilize D-fructose, D-melibiose, esculin, or L-arginine. The isolate exhibited higher MICs for {beta}-lactams, whereas carbapenems and fluoroquinolones showed low MICs. The isolate is capable of forming biofilms and tolerates alkaline conditions, a wide range of temperatures, and different oxygen concentrations. Altogether, this report emphasizes the relevance of additional proteomics- and genomics-based approaches to clarify unusual bacterial infections and describes a new Pannonibacter species with distinct features and the potential to cause opportunistic infections.

papers.title: Cryo-EM Structure of Mycobacteriophage D29 Reveals a Specialized Portal-Capsid Junction and a Unique 13-Subunit Baseplate Collar
papers.abstract: Mycobacteriophages are promising agents against drug-resistant mycobacterial infections, yet their structural organization and host-recognition mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we determined cryo-EM structures of the capsid, connector, tail tube, and baseplate of the lytic, broad-host-range mycobacteriophage D29, revealing a near-complete virion architecture. At the capsid-portal interface, five copies of the previously uncharacterized protein gp19.1 bridge adjacent capsid subunits around the dodecameric portal, potentially reinforcing the symmetry-mismatched vertex. At the baseplate, 13 copies of gp6 assemble into a collar surrounding the sixfold-symmetric gp23-gp27 core. Remarkably, this 6:13 symmetry mismatch is accommodated through six distinct gp6- gp27 interfaces involving 12 gp6 subunits, leaving one subunit largely disengaged from the core. This asymmetric organization produces a tilted, outward-flaring collar that presents an extensive surface with the potential to engage the host cell. Whole-cell binding and plaque-competition assays further implicate the gp6 collar and the flexible trimeric central fiber gp31 in host recognition. Together, these findings reveal distinct structural adaptations at symmetry-mismatched interfaces and provide a structural framework for understanding mycobacteriophage assembly and host engagement.

papers.title: Antibody design across observed and forecasted antigenic evolution
papers.abstract: The therapeutic efficacy of antibodies is often limited by the evolution of their targets. Designing or eliciting antibodies that withstand such evolution is challenging as their binding interfaces must accommodate antigenic variation. Here, we introduce Germinal Multi, a computational framework for de novo antibody design and rescue that jointly optimizes a single paratope against multiple antigenic variants. We applied Germinal Multi to cancer and viral antigens, targeting both observed antigenic variation and prospective antibody escape. Multi-target optimization yielded antibodies that bound resistance-associated EGFR variants or that neutralized antigenically distinct historical SARS-CoV-2 variants, with recognition extending to variants withheld from the design process. Beyond acting on observed evolution, we redesigned the broadly neutralizing antibody BD55-1205 to restore neutralization of a prospective escape variant engineered with guidance from an evolutionary forecasting model, while preserving activity against the parental variant. Successful candidates were identified after screening tens of designs per campaign. Together, these results establish multi-target computational design as a strategy for generating antibody breadth across observed antigenic variation and demonstrate the potential of evolutionary forecasting to guide antibody redesign against prospective escape.

papers.title: High-throughput microarray analysis provides new insight into optimising Rubisco yield from diverse plants
papers.abstract: Interest in plant-based proteins is increasing due to environmental, ethical, and health considerations. Ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase (Rubisco), the most abundant protein on Earth, is present in all green leafy biomass and possesses excellent nutritional and functional properties. Despite its potential, Rubisco remains underutilised because extraction methods are often costly, inefficient, and influenced by species-specific differences. Moreover, the impact on Rubisco yield of cell wall-protein interactions remains poorly understood. We applied Microarray Polymer Profiling (MAPP), a high-throughput platform for simultaneous polysaccharide and protein mapping, to characterise diverse leafy biomass sources. This approach revealed interspecies variation and glycan-protein interactions that influence protein extractability and these insights inform biomass selection and optimisation of extraction protocols to improve Rubisco yield. MAPP was also used to evaluate the effects of carbohydrate-active enzymes on Rubisco recovery through targeted cell wall modification.

papers.title: NRF2-driven thiol metabolism creates a selective vulnerability to selenite
papers.abstract: NRF2 hyperactivation caused by mutations in KEAP1 or NFE2L2 occurs in 20-30% of non-small cell lung cancers and confers therapy resistance. Here we show that NRF2-driven metabolic reprogramming creates a selective vulnerability to selenite. NRF2-dependent thiol export promotes the extracellular reduction of selenite to selenide. Our data support a model in which selenide enters cells and reaches mitochondria, where sulfide-quinone oxidoreductase uses selenide and glutathione to generate the selenopersulfide GS-SeH. A four-hour pulse of selenite was sufficient to induce cell death after washout, consistent with a selenium redox cycle that consumes NADPH and regenerates selenide. Within hours, selenite abolished aconitase activity and impaired mitochondrial respiration. The resulting cell death occurred independently of apoptosis, ferroptosis, pyroptosis, necroptosis and disulfidptosis. In mice, a selenite-rich diet selectively suppressed the growth of NRF2-hyperactive tumors. These findings identify an NRF2-driven metabolic vulnerability and support further investigation of selenite as a therapeutic strategy for NRF2-hyperactive cancers.

papers.title: Multimodal Liquid Biopsy Improves Longitudinal Circulating Tumor DNA Detection in Children with Central Nervous System Tumors
papers.abstract: Background: Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) is a promising biomarker for pediatric central nervous system (CNS) tumors, but limitations in sensitivity and universally accepted detection criteria remain. We evaluated multimodal ctDNA detection using a novel composite scoring framework integrating mutation, copy number, and fragmentomic analysis in longitudinal plasma and CSF samples from children with CNS tumors. Methods: Tumor, blood and/or CSF samples were collected from pediatric CNS tumor patients. DNA was extracted from plasma, CSF, tumor, and whole blood. All samples underwent targeted and whole genome sequencing. Plasma and CSF samples were evaluated for ctDNA positivity--defined by a composite score [≥]2--utilizing a tri-modal approach of whole genome sequencing for copy number alterations and fragmentomics and targeted sequencing. Results: The cohort included 28 patients: medulloblastoma (39%), diffuse midline glioma (25%), high-grade glioma (18%), pilocytic astrocytoma (11%), and ependymoma (7%). A total of 140 plasma and 27 CSF samples were collected longitudinally. Combining all three modalities identified ctDNA in 70% of CSF and 17% of plasma samples, exceeding rates achieved by any single modality alone. Post-diagnosis plasma ctDNA positivity was significantly associated with worse progression-free and overall survival. CSF demonstrated significantly higher ctDNA signal intensity than plasma across all assay modalities. Conclusions: A multimodal composite scoring approach improves longitudinal ctDNA detection in pediatric CNS tumors. Although CSF remains the most sensitive biofluid, plasma ctDNA reflects disease progression in select patients. These findings support integrated, multimodal liquid biopsy strategies for disease monitoring and highlight the need for prospective validation of standardized detection criteria.

papers.title: Global effects of the guanine quadruplex binding ligands Pyridostatin and TMPyP4 on microRNA regulation in response to ionizing radiation in HeLa cells
papers.abstract: Guanine quadruplexes (G4s) are secondary structures in DNA and RNA that regulate a wide range of biological processes. Small molecules that assist in formation, stabilization or destabilization of G4s indirectly alter the cellular functions governed by these structures. Pyridostatin (PDS) and TMPyP4 are two well-characterized G4-binding ligands that have been shown to modulate various cellular functions, particularly in cancer cells. However, their effects on microRNAs (miRNAs), which are key regulators of post-transcriptional gene expression, remain poorly understood. HeLa cells treated either with PDS or TMPyP4 and gamma radiation were subjected to small RNA sequencing. Analysis results revealed a higher overall small RNA content in PDS treated cells, whereas TMPyP4 treated cells exhibited a greater number of differentially expressed miRNAs following gamma radiation exposure. Target gene analysis of the top differentially regulated miRNAs revealed that molecular functions related to DNA/nucleic acid binding activities of various factors, including RNA polymerase II cis-regulatory region sequence-specific binding activity, were largely affected. Furthermore, KEGG pathway enrichment studies suggested that observed changes may result from alterations in signal transduction pathways in cells treated with G4 ligands and gamma radiation compared to untreated control cells. Additionally, G4 ligand treatment altered the cellular expression levels of histone modifying enzymes, including histone deacetylases and methyltransferases. This finding suggest that the two G4 binding ligands- PDS and TMPyP4 differentially regulate miRNA expression profiles, histone modifying enzymes and associated biological pathways in HeLa cells.

papers.title: Evolutionary dynamics of RNA viruses during persistent infection in Drosophila melanogaster
papers.abstract: Persistent viral infections provide an extended window for viral evolution, yet their intra-host trajectories across the host lifespan remain underexplored. Here, we tracked the longitudinal evolution of three single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) viruses (Drosophila A virus [DAV], Drosophila C virus [DCV], and Nora virus) and one double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) virus (Bloomfield virus) during persistent infection in Drosophila melanogaster. By analyzing viral populations across early, intermediate, and late infection stages, we mapped dynamic shifts in the viral quasispecies and the emergence of adaptive mutations. These data demonstrate that long-term persistence drives viral evolution in a viral species-specific manner. DAV evolution was defined by clonal interference, driven by the continuous turnover of competing haplotypes. Nora virus exhibited prolonged evolutionary stasis punctuated by a late-stage sweep, suggesting adaptation to the senescing host environment. In contrast, standard DCV populations were locked under strong purifying selection, where no adaptive mutations were detected. However, this constraint collapsed in high-titer DCV infections, triggering extensive mutational diversification. Distinct from the ssRNA dynamics, the multi-segmented dsRNA Bloomfield virus maintained higher sequence fidelity and a stable genomic formula. Ultimately, these results demonstrate that viral evolution during persistent infection is governed by the interplay between specific host-pathogen interactions and the physiological decline of the host.

papers.title: MERTK and RAC1P29S Drive Melanoma Cannibalism of T cells
papers.abstract: Metastatic melanoma cells are cannibalistic, engulfing living and dead lymphocytes, but the molecular mechanisms that drive this behavior, including how they recognize their targets, are unknown. RAC is a Rho family GTPase that plays a key role in F-actin dynamics. RAC1P29S is a hyperactivating driver mutation that is common in melanoma where it promotes proliferation, motility, and therapy-resistance. Here we show that RAC1P29S melanoma cells engulf more Jurkat T cells than an isogenic RAC1WT revertant line. Live imaging captured lamellipodial dynamics and whole-cell engulfment in real time. An inhibitor screen across RAC1P29S and RAC1WT patient-derived lines showed that cannibalism requires the phosphatidylserine receptor MERTK. A RAC1P29S line lacking detectable MERTK was not cannibalistic, indicating that RAC1 hyperactivity amplifies a specific, receptor-mediated response. RAC1P29S lines are sensitive to RAC and Arp2/3 inhibition. We propose a "grip and gulp" model in which MERTK provides the grip and Arp2/3-driven branched actin the gulp.

papers.title: Ultra-small bacteria and their phages discovered through metagenomics in a sub-arctic degrading permafrost ecosystem
papers.abstract: Patescibacteriota is a diverse bacterial phylum characterized by ultra-small cell size, streamlined genome, incomplete metabolism and episymbiotic lifestyle. While Patescibacteriota have been detected across a wide range of ecosystem types, their phages are not widely described. We utilized metagenomics to explore these less characterized parts of the microbiome in a sporadic permafrost ecosystem, with samples from palsa and peat soils, small ponds and streams. We retrieved 33 high-quality metagenome assembled genomes (MAGs) of Patescibacteriota, mainly from the classes Minisyncoccia and Saccharimonadia. Minisyncoccia was a dominant class in the thawing soils and thaw ponds, whereas the Saccharimonadia was more abundant in the frozen palsa soil layers. The distribution of the Patescibacteria classes was also reflected in their metabolic potential. For example, gluconeogenesis pathway was complete only in MAGs from the class Minisyncoccia, whereas cytochrome o ubiquinol oxidase was mainly found from the MAGs of the class Saccharimondia. The viral community analysis yielded 16 354 viral operational taxonomic units (vOTUs), which represented mainly tailed dsDNA viruses from the class Caudoviricetes. Based on genome size, 16 vOTUs were qualified as jumbophages and one as a megaphage. Similar to the bacterial community, the viral community composition differed across sample types. The most common hosts for bacterial viruses were phyla Pseudomonadota, Acidobacteriota and Actinomycetota. A further 196 vOTUs were in silico linked to Patescibacteriota hosts. The Patescibacteriota phages were diverse, with only two vOTUs representing the same genus. The relative abundance of Patescibacteriota-associated phages was especially high in frozen palsa soils, largely following the same pattern of abundance as Patescibacteriota.

papers.title: Thermopriming prewires orchestrated regulatory programs to enhance heat stress adaptability
papers.abstract: - Plants can remember earlier stress exposures (priming), which improves tolerance to later, more severe stress. How this stress memory is organised in crops remains largely unresolved. - We studied five-day-old rice seedlings subjected to severe heat stress with or without thermopriming, combining phenotyping, time-resolved transcriptomic and epigenomic profiling with systems biology approaches and targeted molecular experiments. - Compared with unprimed seedlings, primed seedlings showed a restrained, lower-entropy transcriptional response spanning diverse biological processes. This response was driven by fewer transcription factors that modulate regulons for both stress response and growth, together contributing to better adaptability to severe stress. - Primed seedlings maintained global H3K27me3 levels, which declined in unprimed seedlings, linking retention rather than removal of this mark to the restrained response. - Priming led to the accumulation of memory chaperone transcripts, enabling a rapid rise in protein abundance under severe stress. This supports better post-translational regulation, alongside the coordinated transcriptional response. Overall, thermopriming establishes pre-wired programmes that enhance adaptability through regulatory order and speed, not amplitude, and repressive-mark retention, not removal, during early development. These findings have implications for (i) understanding heat stress memory in addressing climate change driven heat extremes, and (ii) engineering climate-resilient crops.

papers.title: Regulation of the Epstein-Barr Epigenome by Histone Variant MacroH2A
papers.abstract: Histone variants play an important role in regulating chromatin dynamics of Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV). Here, we investigate the role of histone variant macroH2A in EBV chromatin structure, gene expression and copy number control during latent infection. ChIP-seq analysis in EBV+ SNU719 gastric carcinoma and Mutu I Burkitt lymphoma cells revealed that macroH2A was most enriched at repetitive DNA elements, including oriLyt, BHLF1, LF3 and terminal repeat (TR) regions of the EBV genome. MacroH2A depletion in EBV-associated gastric cancer cell line SNU719 led to a small increase in some viral lytic genes and increase in viral DNA copy number. RNAseq transcriptomics after macroH2A depletion identified major perturbations in cellular gene pathways, including beta-catenin/TCF signaling and chromatin remodeling. Depletion of macroH2A during EBV lytic reactivation reduced EBV lytic gene activation, but increased EBV DNA copy number. Previous study demonstrated a colocalization and cooperative binding between histone variant H2A.Z and EBNA1. We now show that depletion of macroH2A causes an increase in both H2A.Z and EBNA1 at oriP and cellular binding sites for EBNA1. We also found that gammaH2AX localizes to oriP and that this depends on macroH2A. Finally, we show that CRISPR/Cas9 knockout of macroH2A increases the replication and episome maintenance of oriP-containing plasmids. Taken together, these findings indicate that macroH2A localizes to the repetitive elements of EBV, including oriLyt, and can function to limit H2A.Z and EBNA1 binding at oriP, which alters DNA damage signaling at oriP and limits episomal replication. These findings provide a novel role for macroH2A in maintaining EBV copy number and genome integrity.

papers.title: A new cell type facilitated live-bearing and multiple independent origins of placentation in fish
papers.abstract: The origin of new organs has fascinated biologists since Darwin. Yet the molecular and evolutionary steps that give rise to new organs remain difficult to resolve, largely because most organs have ancient origins. The fish family Poeciliidae offers a rare exception. Within poeciliids, placentas have independently evolved at least nine times, including within the last ~10 million years. Here, we study the molecular and cellular drivers of five independent origins of a placenta, using pairs of sister species with and without a placenta. We identified a new maternal cell type that emerged in the common ancestor of poeciliids and likely enabled the family to transition from egg-laying to live-bearing through egg retention. This new cell type originated by partly co-opting the existing gene regulatory network of another ovarian cell type. Subsequently, this same new maternal cell type, together with the embryonic yolk sac, was repeatedly and independently co-opted to form a placenta in all five origins. The evolution of these placentas involved high levels of convergence at the pathway level (e.g., lipid metabolism and vesicle-mediated transport), although these functional changes relied primarily on distinct genes across species. Our analyses show how the evolution and modification of a new cell type enabled the evolution of live birth and placentation, providing the cellular and genetic foundations for the repeated evolution of a new organ.

papers.title: cWnt signaling regulates the early proliferative response and the differentiation of the neural, muscle and parenchymal tissues during planarian whole-body regeneration
papers.abstract: Organizers, or signaling centers, play a central role in coordinating tissue growth, patterning, and differentiation during development and regeneration. In particular, organizers that arise during the regeneration of specific animal structures typically involve components of the canonical Wnt (cWnt) pathway and contribute to tissue growth and differentiation. However, how organizers and the cWnt pathway promote these processes in animals capable of whole-body regeneration remains poorly explored. Here, we analyze organizer functions in planarians, which can regenerate any missing body part from a population of adult pluripotent stem cells. The tips of the planarian body have been proposed to act as organizers. Here we demonstrate the organizing capacity of these tips by showing that anterior or posterior tips grafted into a host animal induce the formation of a patterned head or tail, respectively. Given that the cWnt inhibitor Notum and the activator Wnt1 define these tip regions, we next investigate the role of cWnt signaling in promoting growth and cell differentiation. Our results reveal that cWnt inhibition anteriorly and activation posteriorly are required to promote stem cell proliferation during regeneration. Furthermore, we show that repression and activation of cWnt signaling through {beta}catenin-1 and apc silencing, respectively, can rescue regeneration in sublethally irradiated planarians. Moreover, we show how cWnt signaling at posterior wounds is necessary for the differentiation of specific cell types, including neurons, muscle, and parenchymal cells. Together, our findings identify cWnt signaling as a key regulator of growth and cell differentiation within planarian organizing regions and provide new insight into how organizers control whole-body regeneration.

papers.title: Whole embryo barcoding reveals convergent origins of mesodermal cells during mammalian gastrulation
papers.abstract: Classical fate-mapping and recent single-cell trajectory studies have suggested that mesoderm diversification during gastrulation proceeds through progressive fate bias and branching lineage segregation. Here, we combine inducible CRISPR-based lineage recording with single-cell RNA sequencing to reconstruct clonal relationships across mouse embryos barcoded at primitive streak onset and analyzed at early organogenesis. Mesodermal clones diverged after streak formation, but their developmental outputs remained extensively overlapping, revealing a clonal architecture that is not a simple branching lineage tree. Using sampling-aware statistical models, we quantify distinct clonal origins of paraxial mesoderm across the anterior-posterior axis, show that endothelial cells arise from multiple mesoderm origins but demonstrate transcriptional differences that correspond to anatomical position and clonal lineage, and identify clonal sharing between extra-embryonic mesoderm and embryonic derivatives, including cardiac lineages and a shared hindlimb-allantois progenitor. In the heart, progenitors corresponding to classical heart fields remain multipotent, contributing both myocardial and non-myocardial cell types. Together, our findings support a model in which mesodermal diversity is assembled through spatially distinct, fate-biased progenitor pools whose descendants converge on shared cell states. Our findings challenge simple branching models of mesoderm diversification and provide a clonal framework for understanding how tissue diversity emerges in the embryo.

papers.title: A PI3K-RAC1 signaling axis downstream of mutant TIE2 promotes endothelial dysfunction in venous malformation
papers.abstract: Background: Activating mutations in the endothelial receptor tyrosine kinase TIE2 are a cause of venous malformations (VMs), primarily through dysregulated PI3K/AKT signaling. However, the downstream mechanisms linking constitutively active mutant TIE2 to enlarged vascular lumens, endothelial dysfunction and VM remain incompletely understood. Here, we investigated the role of RAC1 signaling in mutant TIE2 p.L914F driven VM. Methods: Human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) expressing wild-type TIE2 or constitutively active mutant TIE2-L914F were analyzed using RAC1 GTP pull-down assays, immunoblotting, and endothelial cell (EC) 2D and 3D functional assays. The role of RAC1 was evaluated using the RAC1 inhibitor NSC23766 in vitro and in vivo xenograft model of VM. Results & Conclusions: ECs expressing mutant TIE2-L914F showed increased active GTP-bound RAC1. TIE2-L914F ECs exhibited cytoskeletal changes with enhanced lamellipodia formation and maturation, accompanied by increased migration. Pharmacological inhibition of RAC1 significantly attenuated the aberrant vascular lumen area and migration in the mutant TIE2 ECs. Mechanistically, we showed that RAC1 hyperactivation is PI3K-dependent but not MEK/ERK-dependent. Consistent with these findings, RAC1 inhibition significantly reduced vascular lesion formation in a xenograft model of VM with TIE2-L914F ECs. Our study identifies RAC1 as a downstream mediator of TIE2-L914F driven endothelial dysfunction. These results establish a previously unrecognized PI3K-RAC1 signaling axis in the pathogenesis of TIE2-mutated VMs.

papers.title: A living organism-level model of subcellular architecture across adult life reveals a midlife architectural state shift
papers.abstract: Many features of subcellular organelle architecture change throughout life and influence aging. However, our understanding of this structural dynamism relies on single cell systems or comparisons between data sets focused on a limited number of organelles or timepoints. To overcome this barrier, we developed Multiorganelle Mapper (MoMA), a C. elegans strain enabling simultaneous imaging of six organelles across all somatic cell types in fully intact, living animals via fluorescence microscopy. We use MoMA to generate an organism-level in vivo map of subcellular architecture throughout adult life to understand how and why organelle organization changes with age. Aging drives a widespread and consistent shift in subcellular architecture throughout the body. Strikingly, most of this remodeling does not accumulate progressively, but emerges abruptly within individuals at midlife, an inflection point we term the midlife architectural state shift (MASS). Through a targeted RNAi screen, we show the MASS is not unique to aging, but instead resembles a generalized reactive state which can be triggered by a range of distinct homeostatic challenges. Finally, we show the MASS both coincides with and can be driven by midlife physiological changes, suggesting that this remodeling may largely reflect a coordinated reaction to the aged organismal state. Together, we present MoMA as a practical approach for visualizing subcellular architecture at organismal scale and demonstrate how it can be used to uncover principles underlying the dynamic regulation of subcellular architecture throughout life.

papers.title: Virucidal Star Polymer Disrupts Alphavirus Infection in Aedes Mosquitoes
papers.abstract: Mosquito-borne alphaviruses represent an increasing global health threat, yet there are currently no antiviral interventions capable of targeting both the vertebrate host and mosquito vector. Here, we investigated the antiviral potential of the heparan sulfate proteoglycan-mimicking zwitterionic polymer ZP12 against alphavirus infection in Aedes aegypti mosquitoes. ZP12 exhibited potent antiviral and virucidal activity against Ross River virus (RRV) and Semliki Forest virus (SFV) in C6/36 mosquito cells. Antiviral activity was retained in ex vivo mosquito gut cultures, where both high (100 g/mL) and low (0.5 g/mL) concentrations significantly reduced RRV replication, with viral titres reduced by up to five orders of magnitude at peak infection. Delayed-treatment studies demonstrated that ZP12 retained antiviral activity after infection had been initiated, although efficacy declined as treatment was delayed. To evaluate prophylactic delivery, mosquitoes were exposed to ZP12 through sugar feeding prior to viral challenge. While this approach did not directly protect against subsequent gut infection, follow-up experiments demonstrated that ZP12 remained biologically active within the mosquito, suggesting that limited delivery to the midgut rather than loss of antiviral activity restricted efficacy. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that ZP12 is a potent antiviral and virucidal agent against alphaviruses in mosquito cells and tissues and supports its further development as a transmission-blocking strategy for arboviral control.

papers.title: A Luciferase Reporter of Ester Prodrug Delivery to the Cytosol of Intracellular Mycobacteria
papers.abstract: The bacterial cell envelope restricts access to cytoplasmic targets and is a principal reason that otherwise potent antibacterial compounds fail in cells. Masking an anionic carboxylic acid as an ester is a common way to cross that barrier, but the strategy succeeds only if the target organism also hydrolyzes the ester once the compound arrives. These two requirements, permeation and intracellular unmasking, are rarely measured together in live bacterial cells, and existing reporters cannot specify where unmasking occurred. Here we describe a bioluminescent platform that resolves both steps in real time in live mycobacteria using carboxylate esters of D-luciferin. Luciferase requires that an ester both reach the bacterial cytoplasm and be hydrolyzed there, which makes light a compartment-specific readout of productive delivery. Across a series of alkyl esters in Mycobacterium smegmatis, chain length governed permeation while branching adjacent to the carbonyl governed esterase processing, indicating that the two parameters can be tuned independently. The n-butyl ester gave the strongest signal in broth, in infected macrophages, and in the pathogen Mycobacterium avium, whereas the tert-butyl ester was inert in Mycobacterium avium and unmasking of the whole series was attenuated at phagosomal pH. Ester activation is therefore both species- and compartment-dependent, and masking groups are best selected in the organism and environment in which they must act.

papers.title: Strain-specific early, host-shaped late: the rhizobial transcriptome across symbiosis
papers.abstract: The two ends of the rhizobial symbiotic trajectory have only been described separately. Here we report strand-specific RNA-seq of bacteroids of two strains, each against free-living cells of the same strain and alongside its flavonoid response: Sinorhizobium fredii HH103 from soybean (Glycine max), Glycyrrhiza uralensis and Lotus burttii, and Rhizobium tropici CIAT 899 from common bean (Phaseolus vulgaris) and L. burttii, the one legume both strains nodulate. Between 1877 and 2284 genes respond per strain-host combination, and most of that response is host-common: 1171 of 2855 genes respond in all three hosts of HH103 and 1664 of 2703 in both hosts of CIAT 899. What distinguishes the remainder is host identity rather than nodule type, since HH103 bacteroids from the indeterminate-nodule G. uralensis resemble those from L. burttii more than either resembles those from soybean, its natural host. Nitrogen fixation and the stress response are over-represented in every bacteroid and motility is almost entirely repressed, yet the shared core of CIAT 899 is the only repression-dominated gene set here and its translational machinery is induced where that of HH103 is repressed. Dismantling of the early programme is selective: in HH103 the type III apparatus is switched off, the Nod factor operons are attenuated but retained, and the fixABCX operon under a nod box is amplified, so a nod box does not by itself mark a gene as early. CIAT 899, lacking a type III system and placing no nif/fix gene under flavonoid control, keeps that block flat until the nodule, then engages 26 of its 30 genes. Across genera, 26% of responding orthologue pairs are shared in the bacteroid against 5% in the flavonoid response: each bacterium negotiates entry in a dialect of its own and converges on a shared end state whose amplitude, rather than content, the host modulates.

papers.title: Large language models complement established workflows for mechanistic model construction and refinement in systems biology
papers.abstract: Mechanistic models provide a framework for describing, understanding, and predicting biological processes, but their development requires an interdisciplinary team with expertise in biology, mathematics, and computation. Here we present Octomod, a multi-agent workflow based on large language models (LLMs) that integrates biological knowledge retrieval, model construction, parameter estimation, and hypothesis testing. Built on established software tools, including AMICI and pyPESTO, and community standards, including SBML and PEtab, Octomod supports model development and refinement through natural-language interaction with a user. The agents' proposals must pass defined checks and the user's decision before they are used. Every input, model, check, and decision is recorded, so that model building remains transparent and reproducible. We applied Octomod to four problems. Three used published data and differ in model size and in how much the user guided the run: Octomod constructed a model that matched a published model without user guidance, supported the interactive refinement of a gene-regulatory model, and built models of cell-cell communication that explained the responses of five immune cell types to different stimuli. In the fourth application, on newly generated and unpublished lipidomics data, Octomod helped to determine which processes the measurements could inform, identify unresolved label fluxes, and reduce a supplied model to those processes. Together, these results show how LLMs can strengthen and complement established workflows for constructing and refining biologically informed models.

papers.title: A Mathematical Model Connecting Appetite-Driven Food Intake to Metabolic Changes across Diet and GLP-1RA Treatments in Mice
papers.abstract: Mouse models are widely used to study obesity and the effects of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) on appetite-driven meal responses and eating behaviours. However, connecting these behavioural changes to disease prevention remains limited. One reason is that eating behaviour is often summarised as daily or weekly energy intake, obscuring meal-level dynamics. Here we present a mathematical model of mouse appetite-driven food intake across diets and treatment with the GLP-1RAs semaglutide and exenatide. The model jointly described three studies and passed both qualitative assessments and a statistical {chi}2 test (disagreement<threshold, 348<1111). Predictive performance was subsequently validated using four pre-existing studies and one new study. Finally, the model was used to simulate mouse populations under dietary and GLP-1RA interventions, with predictions showing qualitative agreement with the literature. This work aids preclinical drug discovery, supports mouse study design, and improves understanding of how individual meals accumulate into long-term physiological changes.

papers.title: Chromosome-level genomics and cross-species enzyme screening enable high-titer bakuchiol production in Yarrowia lipolytica
papers.abstract: The diversity of enzymes supporting bakuchiol biosynthesis remains incompletely characterized, limiting the repertoire available for microbial pathway engineering. Here, we combined chromosome-level genomics, cross-species enzyme screening and metabolic engineering to establish high-titer bakuchiol production in Yarrowia lipolytica. We assembled a 471.76-Mb Psoralea corylifolia genome anchored to 11 pseudochromosomes, with a contig N50 of 40.33 Mb. Genome-guided screening and functional validation identified four prenyltransferases from P. corylifolia and Vigna radiata whose N-terminally truncated variants supported bakuchiol production in yeast. These results extend experimental evidence for bakuchiol-producing activity across legume prenyltransferase sequences and species. For PcPT6, corresponding to the previously reported PcPT07, removing 40 N-terminal amino acids increased bakuchiol production by 53% relative to the full-length enzyme. We reconstructed bakuchiol biosynthesis in Y. lipolytica and reinforced aromatic precursor synthesis to increase p-coumaric acid supply. Coordinating mevalonate pathway reinforcement with increased t40PcPT6 gene dosage further improved bakuchiol production. Following fermentation optimization, titers reached 108.29 mg/L in shake flasks and 6.03 g/L in a 7.5-L fed-batch bioreactor. These findings connect an expanded set of functional prenyltransferases with coordinated pathway engineering, enabling gram-per-liter microbial bakuchiol production.

papers.title: Combined heat and drought stress alters chromatin accessibility and primes potato abscisic acid biosynthesis
papers.abstract: Due to climate change, abiotic stresses get increasingly more frequent, in a combined and recurrent manner in the same growing season. Chromatin accessibility enables efficient responses to combined stress and priming for reoccurring stresses. To study the regulatory basis of priming, we profiled chromatin accessibility and gene expression in leaves of two genetically distinct potato cultivars after prolonged heat, drought, waterlogging, and combined heat and drought. We show that most accessibility changes are stress-specific, however, drought stress elicits a distinct transcriptional response as compared to combined heat and drought stress, with strong chaperone induction and dampened abscisic acid signalling, despite water deficit. A second cycle of combined stress reveals transcriptional memory of abscisic acid biosynthesis gene StNCED3 and its transcriptional activator StWRKY33b, providing a new mechanistic insight of abiotic stress memory in a staple crop important for global food security.

papers.title: Leaf ionomic stability shapes drought adaptation in pearl millet
papers.abstract: Pearl millet is a staple cereal of semi-arid West Africa, where early-season water deficit constrains vegetative establishment and yield. While the genetic architecture of the pearl millet foliar ionome has been characterised under well-watered conditions, how this ionome reorganises under drought, and whether this reorganisation has a distinct genetic basis, remains unknown. We profiled the drought-response of 17 foliar elements in 175 diverse pearl millet inbred lines over two seasons in Senegal. The foliar concentration of two co-regulated groups of elements changed reproducibly under early water stress across both years. Leaf ion stability, rather than plasticity, was associated with the maintenance of flowering time and plant biomass, suggesting that drought adaptation in pearl millet relies more on ionomic stability than on adaptive shifts in elemental composition. Among the 17 elements, only potassium showed a significant genotype-by-treatment interaction suggesting that genetic variation contributes to differences in potassium response to drought. Genome-wide association mapping on potassium plasticity in response to drought identified a locus, designated qKP-6, that limits potassium depletion under stress without penalising constitutive potassium levels. This locus represents a candidate region for the genetic control of potassium plasticity under drought. This work provides new insights into the genetic control of mineral nutrition under water deficit in pearl millet, and highlights leaf potassium concentration as a genetically controlled component of drought-responsive ionomic variation with potential implications for drought tolerance.

papers.title: Epigenomic circuits shaping cellular heterogeneity in pleural mesothelioma
papers.abstract: Pleural mesothelioma (PM) is an aggressive and lethal malignancy with current treatments offering limited clinical benefit. In this study, we utilized single-cell chromatin accessibility and transcriptomic profiling of patient-matched samples to infer the epigenomic regulation underlying cellular heterogeneity in PM. High-resolution epigenomic profiling suggested transcriptional regulators with putative pro-tumoral roles in mesothelioma, whose function was experimentally tested using genetic perturbations across four PM cell lines. Furthermore, we observed several putative associations between epigenomic circuits and macrophage ontogeny, a sarcomatoid-like neoplastic state, and a fetal-like endothelial cell state. Our analysis also showed similarities between the chromatin accessibility landscapes of exhausted CD8 T and KLRC1 natural killer cells and identified NR4A2 as a potential shared regulator of dysfunction in both lymphocyte subsets. We further identified a state-specific distal enhancer near NR4A2 and experimentally validated its regulation of NR4A2 expression in Jurkat cells. Together, we provide an epigenomic map of PM and nominate candidate transcription factors and regulatory elements for future functional investigation, including their potential relevance to epigenetic editing strategies to limit tumor growth and enhance anti-tumor immunity.

papers.title: Parallel enterocyte caspase and cytokine responses couple hypoxia to reoxygenation-dependent intestinal regeneration in Drosophila
papers.abstract: Intestinal oxygen availability fluctuates during both normal physiology and disease, yet how the intestinal epithelium adapts to these changing environments remains poorly understood. Using the adult Drosophila intestine, we show that hypoxia and reoxygenation drive distinct phases of an epithelial damage and repair response. Hypoxia induces two parallel responses in largely separate enterocyte populations: an AMPK-p53-dependent response that primes enterocytes for apoptosis, and an independent Upd cytokine response that activates JAK-STAT signaling in intestinal stem cells (ISCs). Despite activation of both pathways during hypoxia, neither apoptosis nor ISC proliferation occurs until oxygen is restored. Upon reoxygenation, enterocyte loss and ISC proliferation proceed together and both are required for recovery of intestinal length. We further show that HIF-1/Sima is dispensable in enterocytes but required in progenitor cells for reoxygenation-induced proliferation. Finally, repeated episodes of hypoxia-reoxygenation shorten lifespan, and this is exacerbated by enterocyte p53 knockdown. Together, these findings indicate that the epithelium adapts to fluctuating oxygen by coordinating damage and repair responses in space and time.

papers.title: Engineered Miniature ParTasR Enables Efficient PAMless Genome Editing
papers.abstract: TIGR-Tas system holds great promise for genome-engineering applications owing to its compact size and PAMless targeting capability. However, its low editing efficiency in mammalian cells severely limits its broader utility. Here, we engineered a highly active variant of ParTasR, termed eTasR, through structure-guided rational design of ParTasR combined with fusion to the exonuclease TREX2. eTasR increased mammalian editing efficiency from the original 4.29% to 48.94% with an average 26.52-fold increase, significantly surpassing the efficiency of SpRY, a reported version of PAM-free nuclease. More importantly, single-AAV delivery enabled efficient Hpd disruption in vivo, resulting in robust phenotypic rescue. Thus, eTasR provides a compact, PAMless and highly efficient platform for genome editing and therapeutic applications.
